examples.title: A switch cleanup that keeps the money for declined orders
examples.summary: Merging one case into its neighbours makes the code shorter, and it still compiles. But a payment captured for a declined order is no longer refunded. This repo happens to have a model-checking unit test written for exactly this property, which also fails; the contract catches it without anyone having thought to write that test.

examples.title: A refactor believed equivalent that changes null handling
examples.summary: A nested switch was replaced by a one-line conditional. The agent that wrote it believed the two were equivalent, and every existing unit test passes. They differ on one input: a null status no longer throws.

examples.title: Logging a timestamp makes the decision unverifiable
examples.summary: Appending the current time to a reason string looks like harmless diagnostics. It makes the state machine depend on the clock, so its behaviour can no longer be proved, and the verifier refuses.

examples.title: An equivalent refactor passes without touching the contract
examples.summary: The same simplification as example 002, written with `default ->` instead of `==`. It really is equivalent, so the verifier proves it and the build passes.

examples.title: An intended change, reviewed as a one-line contract diff
examples.summary: Product asks for a clearer message when a customer cancels during payment. The developer changes the code and regenerates the contract, and the pull request shows exactly one changed outcome.

examples.title: A per-seat discount that rounds differently from the per-total one
examples.summary: The group discount is moved from the order total to the unit price, so that tickets can show what each seat cost. It reads as the same arithmetic, and the unit tests pass. The prover finds prices where the two versions differ by a few cents, over an input space of 2^96 values that no test could sweep.
notes: A one-cent rounding drift across 2^96 inputs: no type system and no sampled test can be relied on to find it.

examples.title: A doubled group discount, proved to change only groups
examples.summary: Product doubles the group discount from 10% to 20%. The developer declares that the change affects holds of six seats or more and nothing else, and the prover confirms it for every price and every smaller seat count. The pull request's claim becomes a checked fact.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: equivalent on every input outside the declared change
notes: Proves that a pricing change touches only the groups it says it touches, which is the claim a reviewer would otherwise take on trust.

examples.title: A new tier, written as one formula, also changes groups of six and seven
examples.summary: Product adds 20% off for eight seats or more. The developer writes it generally, a percentage per tier and one formula, and the pull request says that only eight seats or more are affected. The prover disagrees, and shows a group below eight seats whose price changed by a cent.

examples.title: A codec that loads whatever class a Kafka message names
examples.summary: To let one consumer decode messages of either family, the codec writes the Java class name into every payload and resolves it with Class.forName when reading. Round-trip tests pass. The module's capability contract now lists reflection, with the call site: the shape of the Jackson and XStream deserialization CVEs, caught without a CVE database.
notes: The codec starts loading classes named by Kafka messages: a deserialization gadget that a capability contract catches as one new capability.

examples.title: A codec setting that changes payloads but not what the module can do
examples.summary: Message properties are now written in alphabetical order, so that payloads in logs and dead-letter topics diff cleanly. The wire format changes, but the module reaches exactly the same JDK capabilities and libraries as before, and the capability contract passes untouched.

examples.title: Skipping one query in a Kafka listener strands a customer's money
examples.summary: When a payment is captured, the ticketing service counts the seats the order's hold still has before it decides. A developer removes that query: the hold was checked when the order was placed. No unit test covers the listener. The model checker finds a nine-step run across two customers, two services, Kafka and the clock after which a customer is charged, owns no seat, and the event that would have refunded them sits in a dead-letter topic.
notes: The Box Office model (`apps/boxoffice/spec`) has one action per service transaction, relay and clock tick, and TLC checks the README's safety invariants over every interleaving within small bounds. The order state machine in the model is generated from its B8 contract, so the model runs the proven bytecode behaviour.
The nine-step interleaving in which a paid customer loses both their seat and their refund.

examples.title: Deleting the hold sweeper, proved safe for every interleaving
examples.summary: The scheduled job that releases expired holds looks load-bearing: without it, seats of expired holds stay marked HELD. A developer deletes it anyway, and the model checker confirms that every safety invariant still holds in every reachable state, because the rest of the system already treats an expired hold as free.

examples.title: A "longest log wins" vote rule lets a Raft leader overwrite committed entries
examples.summary: Raft's election restriction compares the last log entry's term first and its index second. A developer rewrites it the intuitive way round: the candidate with more entries has seen more history, so index first, term to break ties. Every unit test passes. The prover finds a voter and a candidate for which the old rule refuses the vote and the new one grants it, which is the configuration in which a leader can overwrite an entry the cluster already committed.
notes: A vote rule rewritten as "longest log wins" elects a leader that overwrites committed entries.

examples.title: A leader that ignores newer terms in replies keeps serving a term the cluster has left
examples.summary: Raft's rule for every server is one line: a message from a newer term makes you a follower. A developer narrows it for leaders, reasoning that a leader learns of a new term from the new leader's heartbeats, not from replies to its own RPCs. The behavioural contract of the role machine, 52 cases derived from the bytecode, changes in exactly one of them, and that one is the deposed-leader case.

examples.title: A majority rewritten as "half, rounded up" lets two quorums miss each other
examples.summary: The property that every quorum system rests on is that two majorities always share a node. The module states it next to the code, as `2 * majority(n) > n`, and the build proves it for every cluster size with a bounded model checker. A developer simplifies `n / 2 + 1` to `(n + 1) / 2`, which agrees on every odd size the tests use. The prover answers with n = 2: two "majorities" of one node each, which need not overlap.
notes: `(n + 1) / 2` is not a majority: two quorums of an even cluster can miss each other.

examples.title: Adding jitter inside the backoff kernel gives a pure module a random number generator
examples.summary: The kernels in this module are pure so that a deterministic simulator can drive the whole cluster through thousands of seeded runs and replay any failure exactly. A developer adds jitter to the backoff, the textbook improvement, by calling `ThreadLocalRandom` inside the kernel, and updates the tests to accept a range. The module's capability contract, which lists every JDK capability its bytecode can reach, gains `randomness`, and the build fails: the module can no longer be replayed.

examples.title: A 2PC coordinator that presumes commit on timeout splits the participants
examples.summary: When the vote collection times out, the coordinator aborts: a participant that has not answered may have given up. A developer softens this: if every vote that did arrive was yes, the missing ones are slow, not opposed, so commit. The one-line contract diff is reviewed and approved. The model checker finds a three-step run in which a participant votes no, its vote is still in flight when the timer fires, "everyone who answered said yes" is true of nobody, and the coordinator commits a transaction that participant has already aborted.
notes: The two-phase-commit model (`apps/quorum/spec/TwoPhaseCommit.tla`) is built like Box Office's: the coordinator's state machine is generated from its B8 contract. An example of this model is checked under every configuration the model lists, and its verdict is the first that fails.
Commits over a participant's no vote that is still in flight.

examples.title: Aborting on the first no vote, proved safe for every interleaving of three participants
examples.summary: The coordinator used to wait for every vote before deciding, holding every participant's locks until the last straggler or the timeout. The developer makes it abort as soon as one no arrives. The regenerated contract changes in one case, the model checker runs every interleaving of three participants, the coordinator, the votes in flight and both timeouts, and every invariant holds in every state. The change is merged on a proof, not on a reviewer's mental model of the protocol.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants and properties hold in 644 states, and under 6 more configurations

examples.title: A skew-tolerant tie-break for last-writer-wins lets replicas keep different values
examples.summary: Last-writer-wins resolution must be a total order on writes, or replicas that see the same two writes in different orders keep different values forever. The module states this as a law: `winner(a, b) == 1 - winner(b, a)` for distinct writes. A developer makes the tie-break tolerate clock skew, treating timestamps within five milliseconds as simultaneous and letting the node id decide. The prover finds two writes from the same node a couple of milliseconds apart that each replica resolves in favour of the one it saw first.

examples.title: A partitioner written with Math.abs sends one key in two billion to a negative partition
examples.summary: A custom Kafka partitioner routes a tenant's records by the hash of its id, so that every record of a tenant lands on the same partition. A developer rewrites Kafka's `toPositive(hash) % n`, with its unexplained bit mask, as `Math.abs(hash) % n`, which says what it means. The module's properties file says every hash lands on a partition of the topic. The prover finds the one `int` whose absolute value is negative, and the tool replays it: the partition is negative, which the producer rejects, and that tenant's records are never sent.
notes: `Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` is negative: one key in two billion goes to a negative partition.

examples.title: A rollback rule rewritten as "unchecked means RuntimeException" commits after an Error
examples.summary: Spring's default rollback rule is that a `RuntimeException` or an `Error` rolls the transaction back and a checked exception does not. The kernel writes it as "anything but a checked exception", and a developer rewrites it in the positive, as "a runtime exception", which is how most people remember the rule. The behavioural contract of the transaction boundary, 22 cases derived from the bytecode, changes in exactly one: a method that dies with an `Error` now commits whatever it had written.
notes: Commits after an `OutOfMemoryError`: "a RuntimeException rolls back" is not "unchecked rolls back".

examples.title: A half-open circuit breaker that closes on the first good probe flaps through an outage
examples.summary: A half-open breaker lets a few probe calls through and closes only once all of them are back with the failure rate under the threshold. A developer, chasing the latency of the calls that queue behind the probes, makes the first successful probe enough to close. The behavioural contract of the breaker, 44 cases derived from the bytecode, changes in two of them, and the state-machine view drawn from the patched code shows HALF_OPEN with its waiting state gone.
notes: Compare 076, the half-open rule that judges probes by failure rate, and 075 and 077, the rules that keep every invariant and still never recover.

examples.title: A switch rewrite of the retry policy stops retrying the 5xx statuses it did not list
examples.summary: The retry policy is four `if` statements, and a developer rewrites them as one switch expression over the status, listing the retryable statuses by name, which reads better and is how the team now writes such tables. The regression proof compares the old and the new bytecode on every input, 2^96 of them, and finds a status in the five hundreds that the old code retried and the switch does not.
notes: The switch rewrite stops retrying the 5xx statuses it did not name.

examples.title: A retry helper that sleeps out the Retry-After delay gives a pure module a thread call
examples.summary: The kernels in this module decide and never wait: the retry policy returns whether to retry, and the client's scheduler does the waiting. A developer adds a convenience that waits out the server's `Retry-After` delay with `Thread.sleep` and then decides, so that a client filter can retry inline. The module's capability contract, which lists every JDK capability its bytecode can reach, gains `threads`, and the build fails: the module can now block the thread it is called on.

examples.title: An idempotency key that executes a retry while the first attempt is in flight pays twice
examples.summary: An `Idempotency-Key` receiver refuses a retry while the first attempt with that key is still in progress, with a 409. Support reports clients stuck in 409 loops after a worker died mid-request, and a developer makes the receiver run the retry instead: if a retry arrives, the first attempt is gone. The one-line contract diff is reviewed and approved. The model checker finds a five-step run in which the first attempt is not gone at all, and the request is executed twice.
notes: The idempotency model (`apps/crosscut/spec`) has a client retrying against an `Idempotency-Key` receiver whose state machine is generated from its contract.

examples.title: Storing a failed attempt's response under its key, proved at-most-once for every retry
examples.summary: The receiver used to release an idempotency key when the attempt under it died, so that the client's retry could run the request again. The developer makes it store the failure as the key's response instead, which is Stripe's semantics: a retry gets the first attempt's outcome, whatever it was. The regenerated contract changes in one case, the model checker runs every interleaving of three attempts against the new rule, and every invariant holds in every state. The change is merged on a proof, not on a reviewer's mental model of retries.

notes: The idempotency model (`apps/crosscut/spec`) has a client retrying against an `Idempotency-Key` receiver whose state machine is generated from its contract.

examples.title: tableSizeFor rewritten with numberOfLeadingZeros, proved equal on all 2^32 inputs
examples.summary: The symbol table rounds a requested capacity up to a power of two with the five-shift bit smear of JDK 8's `HashMap.tableSizeFor`. A developer replaces the smear with the one-line form JDK 11 adopted, `-1 >>> Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros(cap - 1)`. The regression proof compiles both versions into one program and proves them equal on every `int`, with the JDK's own bytecode of `numberOfLeadingZeros` in the proof.

examples.title: A vote rule that lets a voter switch candidates within a term elects two leaders

examples.title: An open breaker that restarts its wait on each refused call never probes under load

A developer makes each refused call start the wait over, so that a caller which keeps hammering a failing dependency holds the breaker open until it stops; the contract changes in one row, from a rejection to a transition that stays open and starts the wait, and the test of the open state is updated to say so. Every safety invariant of the model holds: an open breaker still lets nothing through before its wait, still shields the dependency, still probes a limited number of times. The liveness check, a second configuration of the same model under fairness conditions, finds the run in which the caller never stops: two failures open the breaker, the dependency comes back, and from then on every tick of the clock is answered by a call that starts the wait over. examples.title: A coordinator that aborts the transaction on restart reverses a commit it had sent
examples.summary: A two-phase-commit coordinator logs each phase change before it acts on it, and a restart after a crash reads the log: a logged decision is sent again, since the crash may have come before the broadcast, and no logged decision means abort. A developer collapses the three cases of the recovery rule into one, abort: whatever the coordinator was doing, an abort releases the participants' locks, and a transaction that was about to commit can be retried. The contract diff is one row, a restart in `COMMITTED`, from sending the commit again to aborting. The two-phase-commit model is now checked under two more configurations, in which the coordinator may crash between steps or between logging a decision and sending it, and restarts on the recovery rule, generated from the contract like the decision rule. Under the two the model had, nothing crashes and the row is never taken. Under the third, TLC finds in ten steps a commit that is sent, applied by one participant, and then reversed by the restarted coordinator, which tells the other two to abort; the fourth finds the same step from a state its inductive invariant admits.
notes: The two-phase-commit model (`apps/quorum/spec/TwoPhaseCommit.tla`) is built like Box Office's: the coordinator's state machine is generated from its B8 contract. An example of this model is checked under every configuration the model lists, and its verdict is the first that fails.

`TwoPhaseCommitCrash.cfg` and `TwoPhaseCommitCrashInductive.cfg` let the coordinator crash between steps, or after logging a decision and before sending it, and restart on a recovery rule, the model's second generated operator (`Recovery#decide`).
Reverses a commit a participant has already applied: only a model that lets the coordinator crash can see it.

examples.title: A coordinator with nothing to redo on restart leaves a logged decision unsent forever

The contract diff is two rows, and the change mirrors the rule beside it. Under the two configurations the model had, nothing crashes and the rows are never taken; the inductive invariant is closed under the new rule as well, since every state the run passes through is one it admits. The third configuration, in which the coordinator may crash twice, finds the run in eight steps: two participants vote yes, the coordinator crashes as it counts the first of them, the third participant gives up, and the coordinator restarts, logs the abort that presumed abort calls for, and crashes again before sending it; the second restart finds a logged abort and the new rule has nothing to redo. The two prepared participants hold their locks forever, a liveness failure, reported as a run that stays in its last state. The fourth configuration finds the step that makes it possible, a coordinator up and decided with nothing out.

examples.title: A follower that takes entries after a conflicting previous entry breaks log matching
examples.summary: A Raft follower refuses a leader's entries unless it holds the entry before them, the consistency check of section 5.3, so that the leader backs up one entry at a time until the logs agree. A developer relaxes the check to the previous index existing, whatever entry is there: the leader's later entries overwrite the conflict in due course, the comment says, and a round trip is saved. The tests pass and the contract diff is eight rows. The replication model's first configuration, three servers, three terms and two entries, finds in twelve steps two logs that hold the same entry of term 3 at index 2 over different entries at index 1, which is what the log matching property forbids and what the check exists to prevent; the second, figure 8 of the paper, finds a follower that applies an entry nobody else committed, and the third, three terms and one entry under fairness, the same.
notes: The Raft replication model (`apps/quorum/spec/RaftReplication.tla`) has the logs live, around the follower's append rule and the leader's commit rule as generated operators beside the role machine and the vote rule, and checks log matching, leader completeness and state machine safety, with an action property that no committed entry is ever overwritten. Its configurations are three terms with two entries, and the four terms of the paper's figure 8.

The tests pass, the contract diff is one row, and the model's first configuration, three terms, verifies the change in 25,666 states, and so does the third, under fairness. examples.title: apache/commons-numbers#223: ArithmeticUtils.pow accepts (-2)^31, found and confined from bytecode

examples.title: apache/commons-lang#1750: ArrayUtils.reverse with Integer.MIN_VALUE as the end index

examples.title: apache/commons-lang#1585: ArrayUtils.subarray index arithmetic overflow
examples.summary: A pull request that clamps `ArrayUtils.subarray`'s end index from below, because `end - start` could overflow to a positive size. examples.title: An Idempotency-Key header added to POST /orders drops the request body's validation on the way
examples.summary: Clients already send an `Idempotency-Key` on `POST /concerts/{id}/holds`, so a developer makes `POST /orders` accept the same header, writing the handler's new parameter list by hand. The `@Valid` on the request body does not survive the edit. Every test passes: they post well-formed orders. The module's boundary contract, the routes and the advice on each read from the compiled classes, shows the `POST /orders` line changing from a validated body to an unvalidated one, next to the header that was added.
notes: The first example of approach B12, the boundary contract (`jvmcontract boundaries`, `verify --add boundaries`): where Spring enters a module and the advice on each bean, from the annotations in the class files. The three Box Office modules with Spring annotations carry theirs in `src/contract/boundaries.contract`, checked by `./gradlew check` when `jvmcontract` is on the PATH (`verifyBoundaries`, `updateBoundaries`).

Box Office keeps its transactions programmatic (`Transactions`), so none of the contract's `!` lines (self-invocation of a `@Transactional` method, advice on a private or final method, a checked exception that commits, a lost `@Async` result) occur here; the library's Spring fixtures (`lib/tests/fixtures/spring`) have one of each. An example of a `@Transactional` self-invocation needs a service with `@Transactional` beans: a candidate for Crosscut's framework glue, which the kernels there deliberately leave out.

The runner (`build.py`, `run_boundaries`) compiles the patched module with Gradle and runs `jvmcontract verify` over its `src/contract` directory; it does not use the Gradle build's own `verifyBoundaries` task, so it works without the tool on the PATH of the Gradle daemon. The existing tests are the module's Spring Boot tests, which need Docker for Testcontainers; without it they fail before the change is tested, which the page records as the tests' result, not the verifier's.

The observation specs (`jvmcontract observations --against`, foundations O2), Box Office with this change against Box Office as it is (`lib/tests/observations.rs`, `box_office_examples_compare_as_their_boundary_diffs_say`): `POST /orders` gets two changed obligations. `inputs` names the new `Idempotency-Key` header and, in the body's wire shape, `! constraints on PlaceOrder are not checked: no @Valid on request`. `status` says that before the handler runs the old build answers `MethodArgumentNotValidException` with 400 for a body that fails one of `@NotBlank on PlaceOrder.holdId`, `@NotBlank on PlaceOrder.paymentToken`, and that the new build runs the handler instead. The spec models request validation as an outcome the framework takes before the handler, with the requests it is for, so a dropped `@Valid` is a changed status mapping, not a preserved one.

examples.title: A PaymentVoided event joins the sealed PaymentEvent family without its @JsonSubTypes entry
examples.summary: The payment service voids an order whose refund arrives before any charge, and until now told nobody. A developer adds a `PaymentVoided` record to the sealed `PaymentEvent` interface, publishes it on the void path, and handles it in ticketing, where the compiler insists on the new case of the sealed switch. The `@JsonSubTypes` list on the interface, which names the type id of each event on the wire, is not touched. Every test passes: the compiler checked the Java side, the codec test round-trips the three events it knew about. Jackson writes the new event with the type id `PaymentEvent$PaymentVoided` and the consumer rejects it. The regenerated boundary contract of the `contracts` module shows the new type with a `!` line saying exactly that.
notes: The first example of the wire types in a boundary contract (`jvmcontract boundaries`, `verify --add boundaries`): the JSON shape of each request, response and message type as Jackson encodes it, with `!` lines for the Jackson pitfalls that no test with the same classes on both sides can see. The `contracts` module of Box Office has no Spring annotations; its boundary contract is wire types only, and it is checked by `./gradlew check` like the others when `jvmcontract` is on the `PATH`.

The runner (`build.py`, `run_boundaries`) treats an intended change as a regeneration: it runs `jvmcontract update`, records the contract diff, and reports as the violation any `!` line the regenerated contract has that the old one did not. An unintended change is a plain `verify`, as in example 110.

Jackson 3.1 behaviour, checked with a scratch program against the jars Box Office uses: a permitted subtype missing from an explicit `@JsonSubTypes` is written as `Outer$Inner` and rejected on reading; a sealed interface with `@JsonTypeInfo` and no `@JsonSubTypes` accepts all permitted subtypes under their class names, which the contract reports as a type id that is a class name; a listed subtype without `name` gets the class name too. Jackson 2 does not read permitted subclasses at all, so there the unlisted event fails on reading in every case.

The patch touches three modules (the record, the publisher, the consumer's switch); the runner compiles and checks the `contracts` module, where the subject is. The payment-service tests that exercise the void path are not in this patch, as they were not in the developer's change.

The observation specs (`jvmcontract observations --against`, foundations O2), Box Office with this change against Box Office as it is (`lib/tests/observations.rs`, `box_office_examples_compare_as_their_boundary_diffs_say`): nothing changes in any module's specs. The new `PaymentVoided` is enqueued through the outbox like the other events, so the payment listener's effect has the same call, sites and snapshot paths; its type id is inside the encoded string payload (`objectToSave.payload`), a payload value the static spec doesn't see. The effect stays preserved-to-prove, and only a trace proof over payload values with the codec modeled would refute it. The wire block of the boundary contract is what catches this example; the comparison names it as not observed (`observations::NOT_OBSERVED`).

examples.title: A prod profile raises the hold seat limit under boxoffice.hold.max-seat, a key nothing reads
examples.summary: Production wants a hold to be able to take a whole row, so a profile document for `prod` is added to the ticketing service's `application.yaml` with `boxoffice.hold.max-seat: 12`. The key the code reads is `max-seats`. Spring Boot ignores a key nothing binds, so production keeps the default of 8, and no test runs with the `prod` profile. The module's boundary contract lists each configuration key with the value each profile gives it and who reads it; the regenerated contract has a new line for the mistyped key, with a `!` under it that names the nearest known key.
notes: The first example of the configuration block of a boundary contract (`lib/src/config.rs`): the keys the classes read, the keys the application files set and the keys the class path's configuration metadata declares, cross-checked. The runner passes the module's resource directory with `--resources` and the runtime class path from Gradle's `printRuntimeClasspath` task with `--classpath`, so the metadata in the Spring Boot jars is read; without the class path, every `spring.*` and `server.*` key would be reported as unbound.

The other `!` lines of the block, each in the library's Spring fixtures (`lib/tests/fixtures/spring/resources/application.yaml`): a key the metadata marks deprecated (`spring.data.mongodb.uri` in Spring Boot 4, which no longer binds it and names `spring.mongodb.uri`), a value that is not of the key's type (`ttl: 2 minutes` for a `Duration`, `port: eighty`, an enum constant that does not exist), and a placeholder default that is not (`${holds.retries:many}` for an `int`). A key no file sets is not a problem, since it may come from the environment: it is shown with its default and no value.

The patch changes no Java, so the module compiles as before and the existing tests pass as before; the runner compiles it anyway, since the contract is read from the classes and the files together. The Spring Boot tests of the module need Docker for Testcontainers; without it they fail before the change is tested, which the page records as the tests' result, not the verifier's.

The observation specs (`jvmcontract observations --against`, foundations O2), Box Office with this change against Box Office as it is (`lib/tests/observations.rs`, `box_office_examples_compare_as_their_boundary_diffs_say`): nothing changes in any module's specs: a configuration key's value is not observed by an entry-point spec (`observations::NOT_OBSERVED`). The boundary contract's configuration block is what catches this example.

examples.title: A nested Billing record on PlaceOrder carries @NotBlank constraints that no @Valid leads into
examples.summary: Orders gain billing details for the receipt: a nested `Billing` record with `@NotBlank` and `@Email` on its fields, added to `PlaceOrder` as a `@NotNull` component. The handler validates the request with `@Valid`, so the author expects a blank name or a bad email to be refused. Bean Validation does not step into a nested object unless the property itself carries `@Valid`, so the only check that runs on the billing details is that they are present; every test posts valid ones and passes. The module's boundary contract lists each wire type with its constraints, and the regenerated contract has a `!` line under the new property saying that the constraints on `Billing` are not checked.
notes: The first example of the validation checks on a boundary contract (`lib/src/validation.rs`): a nested type's constraints with no `@Valid` leading into them (this example), a `@RequestBody` taken without `@Valid` or `@Validated` while its type carries constraints, a `@Valid` or `@Validated(G.class)` that leaves out the constraints of other groups, a constraint on a type its validator cannot handle (`@Size` on an `int`, which Hibernate Validator rejects at the first validation with `UnexpectedTypeException`), a null check on a primitive, and constraints on a non-public method of a `@Validated` bean. Each is a `!` line under the property or the handler; the library's Spring fixtures (`lib/tests/fixtures/spring/fixtures/spring/Booking.java`) have one of each.

The contract now writes the constraints inside a type, read from the class file's type annotations (`RuntimeVisibleTypeAnnotations`): `rows: @NotEmpty List<@Pattern(regexp = "[A-Z]") String>` in the ticketing service's `CreateConcert`, which earlier contracts showed as `List<String>`. The type-use constraints are where `List<@Valid Item>` cascades from, so a cascade check needs them.

The patch changes the Java of the module, so the runner compiles it with Gradle, reads the runtime class path through the build's `printRuntimeClasspath` task, and runs `jvmcontract update` then `verify` with `--resources` and `--classpath`. The Spring Boot tests of the module need Docker for Testcontainers; without it they fail before the change is tested, which the page records as the tests' result, not the verifier's.

The observation specs (`jvmcontract observations --against`, foundations O2), Box Office with this change against Box Office as it is (`lib/tests/observations.rs`, `box_office_examples_compare_as_their_boundary_diffs_say`): `POST /orders` gets two changed obligations. `inputs`: the body's wire shape gains `Billing` and `PlaceOrder: billing: @NotNull Billing`, with `PlaceOrder: billing: ! constraints on Billing are not checked: no @Valid on billing`, since the input domain is the preservation contract's. `status`: `MethodArgumentNotValidException` is now also for a body that fails `@NotNull on PlaceOrder.billing`, so a request the old build took is answered 400. That is the change of meaning a person approves. The unchecked `Billing` constraints are new behaviour with no old counterpart, so the comparison names them and doesn't count them as a regression.

examples.title: A @Cacheable on the concert lookup with no @EnableCaching in scope: every call still reads Mongo
examples.summary: A concert does not change after it is created, and every hold and order reads it, so the developer puts `@Cacheable("concerts")` on the store's lookup. The annotation compiles, the context starts, every test passes, and nothing is cached: no configuration in the ticketing service's scope carries `@EnableCaching`, and Spring Boot does not switch caching on by itself. The module's boundary contract has an activation block that names, for each kind of annotation the module uses, what enables it; the regenerated contract has a new line `@Cacheable: nothing enables it` with a `!` line under it.
notes: The first example of the activation block of a boundary contract (`lib/src/activation.rs`): for each family of annotations the module uses (`@Scheduled`, `@Async`, `@Cacheable`, `@PreAuthorize`, `@Secured`, `@RolesAllowed`, `@Transactional`, `@Retryable`, `@Aspect`, `@KafkaListener`, `@RabbitListener`, `@JmsListener`, `@WebFilter`, `@Valid`, `@Validated`, `@Timed`, `@Counted`, `@Observed`), the switch that enables it, or a `!` line when nothing does. The `!` line names the nearest miss when there is one: a class that carries the switch but is not a component, a configuration outside the scanned packages, or an auto-configuration whose `@ConditionalOnClass` or `@ConditionalOnResource` fails (`no TimedAspect bean on a configuration in scope (MetricsAspectsAutoConfiguration defines one, but org.aspectj.weaver.Advice is not on the class path)`). The library's Spring fixtures (`lib/tests/fixtures/spring/fixtures/spring/App.java` and `fixtures/boot/`) have one of each.

What counts as a configuration in scope follows Spring's own rules as far as the class files show them: the local classes with a stereotype (meta-annotations followed, so `@Service` is a `@Component`) in the packages the application class scans (its own, or `scanBasePackages`), the classes of the class path in those packages, the `@Import`s of each, their nested configuration classes, and the auto-configurations the class path's `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` files and `spring.factories` list minus the application's `exclude`s. `@ConditionalOnClass`, `@ConditionalOnMissingClass`, `@ConditionalOnResource` and `@ConditionalOnWebApplication` are evaluated against the class path; `@ConditionalOnBean`, `@ConditionalOnProperty` and `@Profile` are taken as met, so a switch behind a property the contract cannot see is reported as present. Spring Boot 4 lists its auto-configurations per module jar (`spring-boot-kafka`, `spring-boot-transaction`, `spring-boot-validation`), and the walk reads every jar's file.

The example is caching because `@Cacheable` needs no new dependency, so the patch is one annotation. The `@Valid` case is the one developers hit most, since Spring Boot 2.3 moved Hibernate Validator out of the web starter: a build that drops `spring-boot-starter-validation` keeps compiling against `jakarta.validation-api`, and every `@Valid` on every handler goes quiet. In the activation block that is `@Valid: nothing enables it` with `! no Bean Validation provider on the class path (spring-boot-starter-validation adds Hibernate Validator)`.

The patch changes the Java of the module, so the runner compiles it with Gradle, reads the runtime class path through the build's `printRuntimeClasspath` task, and runs `jvmcontract update` then `verify` with `--resources` and `--classpath`. The Spring Boot tests of the module need Docker for Testcontainers; without it they fail before the change is tested, which the page records as the tests' result, not the verifier's.

The observation specs (`jvmcontract observations --against`, foundations O2), Box Office with this change against Box Office as it is (`lib/tests/observations.rs`, `box_office_examples_compare_as_their_boundary_diffs_say`): nothing changes in any module's specs, which is right: with no `@EnableCaching` the `@Cacheable` is inert, every read still happens, and a read is a modeled call, not an observation. The defect is a cache that doesn't work, not a regression of what consumers observe. Advice such as caching is named as not observed (`observations::NOT_OBSERVED`); the activation block of the boundary contract catches it.

examples.title: HoldDocument.idempotencyKey renamed, the query strings not: a retried POST holds the seats twice
examples.summary: The developer renames `HoldDocument.idempotencyKey` to `requestKey`; the IDE renames the component and its javadoc, the hold is built positionally, so nothing else changes and everything compiles. The mapper now stores the key under `requestKey`, while `TicketingStore.holdByIdempotencyKey` still runs `where("idempotencyKey")` and the unique index is still on `idempotencyKey`: the lookup matches nothing, the index covers nothing, and a client that retries `POST /concerts/{id}/holds` with the same `Idempotency-Key` gets a second hold on other seats. The boundary contract's stored types block shows the document's shape and checks every field-name string in the module against it; the regenerated contract has three new `!` lines under `HoldDocument`.
notes: The first example of the stored types block of a boundary contract (`lib/src/store.rs`): the shape of each Spring Data MongoDB document as the mapping layer writes it (the `@Id` or the property named `id` as `_id`, a `@Field` rename as `due: Instant (dueAt)`, `@Transient` and `transient` fields left out, embedded local types as their own `record, embedded` blocks), and under each document a `!` line for every string in the module that names a field it does not have. The strings come from the bytecode: the constant pushed as the field argument of `Criteria.where`/`and`, the `Update` operators (`set`, `unset`, `inc`, `push`, `pull`, `rename`, ...), `Index.on`, `Sort.by` (varargs read back from the array the compiler builds), `Sort.Order.asc`/`desc`, the projection's `include`/`exclude`, and from the annotations: a repository method's `@Query` (`value`, `sort`, `fields`, parsed as the loose JSON Spring accepts, with the `$` operators transparent) and a document's `@CompoundIndex(def)`.

A string names a property by its Java name or its stored name, as Spring's query mapper accepts both (`where("due")` and `where("dueAt")` both reach a `@Field("due") Instant dueAt`), `_id` and the id property's own name both reach the id, a dotted path goes through an embedded type's fields, through a collection or array to its element and through a map to any key, and stops at a leaf: `"assignee.email" is a String, which has no fields`. `$`-segments (`steps.$.done`) and array indices are skipped. The nearest property is suggested when one is within a few edits (`not a field of NoteDocument (createdAt?)`); here `requestKey` is too far from `idempotencyKey` for a hint. The library's Spring fixtures (`lib/tests/fixtures/spring/fixtures/spring/NotesStore.java`, `NoteRepository.java`, `TaskDocument.java`) have one wrong string of each kind.

Which document a string is about is read from the method: the document classes it passes to the template or instantiates. `holdByIdempotencyKey` names `HoldDocument.class` alone, so its line says `not a field of HoldDocument`; the constructor creates indexes for `SeatDocument`, `HoldDocument` and `OrderDocument`, so the two lines from it name all three (the string is a field of none), and the line goes under the first. A private helper that names no document (`makeAvailable()` in the same store) takes the documents of the methods that call it. The checks cover Spring Data MongoDB; JPA queries are JPQL, which Hibernate validates at startup, and derived query methods (`findByHoldId`) are checked by Spring Data at startup, so neither needs a contract line. Aggregation pipelines are not followed: a stage after a `group` names computed fields.

examples.title: GET /holds/{id} now extends the hold it returns: a polling checkout page keeps seats held for ever
examples.summary: The developer makes `GET /holds/{id}` keep the hold alive: `HoldService.get` pushes the expiry of the hold and of its seats forward on every call, so a customer filling in the payment form does not lose the seats under them. The checkout page polls that endpoint for its countdown, so a hold now never expires while a tab is open, a browser's prefetch or a monitor's probe keeps seats off the market, and a retried GET changes state. The boundary contract now says what each entry point reaches (the documents it reads and writes, the topics it sends to, the HTTP calls it makes, the events it publishes); the regenerated contract has `writes HoldDocument, SeatDocument` under the GET and a `!` line: a safe method with side effects.
notes: The first example of the reach lines of a boundary contract (`lib/src/reach.rs`). For every entry point and advised method, the tool follows the calls in the bytecode through the application's own classes (the module and its sibling modules on the class path; a call into Spring, the JDK or a driver is a leaf) and classifies the leaves: the Spring Data templates and repositories, the JPA `EntityManager` and `JdbcTemplate` give `reads` and `writes` (of the class literal passed, else the static type of the entity argument, else the documents the method mentions; a table from the SQL constant), the Kafka, RabbitMQ, JMS and Spring Cloud Stream templates give `sends` (the topic when it is a constant, else `to Kafka`), `RestTemplate`, `RestClient`, `WebClient` and `@HttpExchange` or Feign interfaces give `calls GET /path`, `ApplicationEventPublisher` gives `publishes`. A virtual call goes to every local subtype that overrides the method, a lambda to its body whether or not the receiver runs it: a may-reach approximation, which is the right side to err on for a reviewer.

Two checks read these lines: a `GET` or `HEAD` route that writes, sends, publishes or makes a non-GET call is `! a GET that ...: a safe method with side effects`, and a `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` method that writes is `! @Transactional(readOnly = true) but writes ...: a read-only transaction drops or rejects writes` (Hibernate sets the flush mode to manual and silently keeps the changes, PostgreSQL rejects the statement, MongoDB ignores the flag). A nested class keeps its outer name so the two `Entry` records stay apart.

A method called through reflection or a bean looked up by name is not followed; a data call whose entity argument is a `List` built elsewhere falls back to the documents the method mentions. The GET check is a statement about HTTP semantics, not about this application: a GET that records a metric or refreshes a cache is flagged the same way, and the line is for the reviewer to accept or move.

The change is a feature rather than a refactoring because the keep-alive is what the developer wants; the point of the example is that the contract puts the cost of the shortcut on the page the reviewer reads, as a side effect of a safe method, instead of leaving it to be found when the next concert sells out with half the seats held by abandoned tabs. In an entry point the old build has, a new attempt is a change to its ordered trace: it needs a person's approval or a proof that it is never reached, and the count says so.

examples.title: Payment command sent to Kafka from inside the order transaction: the outbox dropped for a dual write
examples.summary: The developer drops the outbox from the order path: `OrderService.place` sends the `ChargePayment` command to Kafka itself, from inside the MongoDB transaction that records the order, so the payment service hears about the order at once instead of on the relay's next poll. The send is not part of the transaction. A write conflict makes `Transactions.run` retry the work, and each attempt sends a fresh command with a fresh id; a transaction that rolls back after the send has told the payment service to charge for an order that does not exist; a process that dies between the commit and the send leaves an order that waits for a payment nobody was asked for. The boundary contract places every effect with respect to transactions; the regenerated contract has `sends payments.commands` under `POST /orders` and a `!` line: a transaction that sends.
notes: The first example of the transaction placement of the reach lines (`lib/src/reach.rs`): the walk from each entry point carries a scope, outside any transaction, inside one the root opened, or inside a `@Transactional` method of another class, and the effects go into `all`, `outside` and `inside` sets. The root is inside its own transaction when it is `@Transactional` (with a propagation that joins or opens one); a lambda enters the root's transaction when it is an argument of a call to `TransactionTemplate.execute` or `executeWithoutResult`, or to a method (a runner) that reaches either of those or a `@Transactional` method: Box Office's `Transactions.run(Supplier)` calls `template.execute`, and `run(Runnable)` calls that, so a lambda handed to either is inside. A `@Transactional` method of another class on the path takes its effects for itself (its own member in the contract carries them), so the `!` line sits under the service method and not under every route that calls it; a `@Transactional` method of the same class is a self-invocation, which the proxy does not see, and changes nothing.

Four checks read the placement: a send (Kafka, RabbitMQ, JMS, Spring Cloud Stream, SQS, SNS, a `MessageChannel`) inside the root's transaction is `! a transaction that sends to ...` (left alone when `spring.kafka.producer.transaction-id-prefix` is set in an application file, which makes the Kafka producer transactional and synchronises its commit with the database's: not atomic, but not the plain dual write); an HTTP call inside it is `! a transaction that calls POST /...: the call is not part of the transaction, so a rollback does not undo it, and the transaction stays open for the round trip`; an event published with no transaction on the path, when a method of the module (or a sibling) is a `@TransactionalEventListener` for that event type without `fallbackExecution = true`, is `! publishes E outside a transaction: ...`, since Spring drops the event when no transaction is active; and a `@TransactionalEventListener` whose phase is not `BEFORE_COMMIT` and whose reach writes is `! an AFTER_COMMIT listener that writes ...` unless it is `@Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW)` or `@Async`: after the commit the transaction's resources are still bound to the thread and nothing commits again, so a JPA or JDBC write there is never committed (Spring's documentation of `TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT` says the same). The Box Office contracts regenerated unchanged: no module sends from inside `Transactions.run`, the outbox relay sends from a `@Scheduled` method with no transaction, and nothing publishes application events.

What the placement does not know: a transaction driven by hand through a `PlatformTransactionManager`, a lambda a runner takes but runs after its commit (it is placed inside), a `@Transactional` on a Kafka or JMS transaction manager (read as a database transaction, so a send under it is still flagged), and the retry in `Transactions.run`, which is what turns this dual write into a double charge: the `!` line says the send is not part of the transaction, and the reviewer, who knows the helper retries, draws the rest. The writes line also changes in this example (`Outbox.Entry` leaves it), which a reviewer who knows what the outbox is for would stop at on its own; the `!` line is there for the one who does not.

The change is a refactoring in the developer's eyes because the same command reaches the same topic; the page keeps it as `refactor` with the behaviour change marked intended, since the point is the shortcut's cost showing up under the route the reviewer reads. The patch changes the Java of the module, so the runner compiles it with Gradle, reads the runtime class path through the build's `printRuntimeClasspath` task, and runs `jvmcontract update` then `verify` with `--resources` and `--classpath`. The Spring Boot tests of the module need Docker for Testcontainers; without it they fail before the change is tested, which the page records as the tests' result, not the verifier's.

The observation specs (`jvmcontract observations --against`, foundations O2), Box Office with this change against Box Office as it is (`lib/tests/observations.rs`, `box_office_examples_compare_as_their_boundary_diffs_say`): `POST /orders`: the `MongoTemplate.insert` effect is changed (the old build writes `Outbox.Entry` by it inside its transaction and the new one doesn't, with the outbox entry's payload paths gone), and beside it the comparison names what the new build attempts instead: `sends to payments.commands, inside its transaction, in OrderService.lambda$place$0`. The `KafkaTemplate.send` is a new attempt in the route's trace. Statically the comparison sees an effect replaced by another; the dual write and its retry duplicate are for the trace proof (O3) and the boundary contract's `!` line.

examples.title: Hold route variable renamed in the template but not in the parameter: a 500 on every request of it
examples.summary: The developer renames the path variable of `GET /holds/{id}` to `{holdId}`, so the route reads like the OpenAPI description, and leaves the handler's parameter as `@PathVariable String id`. Spring binds a `@PathVariable` by name, the annotation's or the parameter's, at request time: no template of the route has a variable named `id`, so every request of the route ends in `MissingPathVariableException`, a 500. The code compiles, the context starts, and the module's unit tests, which call the service and not the route, pass. The boundary contract now checks each handler's request binding; the regenerated contract has a `!` line under the renamed route: `@PathVariable id matches no variable in /holds/{holdId}`.
notes: The first example of the request binding checks (`lib/src/binding.rs`), which read a handler's parameter annotations against its routes and its bytecode. A `@PathVariable`, `@RequestParam`, `@RequestHeader`, `@CookieValue` or `@MatrixVariable` binds by name: the annotation's `value` or `name`, else the parameter's name as the `MethodParameters` attribute records it (what `javac -parameters` writes and what Spring reads by reflection; the `LocalVariableTable` of `-g`, which Spring 6.0 fell back to, is not read by 6.1). Four things are `!` lines: a `@PathVariable` whose name is a variable of no template of the route (this example; `{id:\\d+}` and `{*rest}` count as `id` and `rest`, and a `Map` parameter takes every variable and needs no name); a named binder on a parameter whose name is not in the bytecode, which fails every request with a 500 (compile with `-parameters`, as the Spring Boot Gradle and Maven plugins do by default and Box Office's conventions do by hand, or name it in the annotation); a `required = false` binder with no `defaultValue` on a primitive, which cannot be null when the request leaves it out (a 500 instead of the 400 a missing required parameter gets); and two `@RequestBody` parameters, the second of which always reads an empty body.

Two handlers on one route are found across the module: the same route rendered identically on two methods (`GET /tasks/open` twice) is a duplicate Spring refuses at startup (`IllegalStateException: Ambiguous mapping`), reported under both; the same pattern under different variable names (`/tasks/{id}/owner` and `/tasks/{key}/owner`) registers twice, since the patterns differ as strings, and every request that matches both finds them equally specific, so Spring throws `Ambiguous handler methods` for it, a 500. The pattern key drops the variable names and the constraints inside the braces; `consumes`, `produces`, `params` and `headers` stay in the key, so two routes that differ in them are not reported (Spring tells them apart by the request's headers). The Box Office contracts regenerated unchanged: every `@PathVariable` of the three modules names a variable of its route, the modules compile with `-parameters`, and no two handlers share a pattern.

What the checks do not know: a mapping annotation of the application's own composed of `@RequestMapping` (its elements are not read as paths), a `@PathVariable` on a `@ModelAttribute` or an `@InitBinder` method, a route whose template comes from a constant in another class (the string is in the annotation either way, so this one is fine), a parameter name available to Spring through a `ParameterNameDiscoverer` of the application's own, and the HEAD and OPTIONS requests Spring answers for a GET route. The `required = false` check reads `required` and `defaultValue` as written on the annotation, and `Optional<T>` is an object, not a primitive, so it passes.

The runner compiles the module with Gradle, reads the runtime class path through the build's `printRuntimeClasspath` task, and runs `jvmcontract update` then `verify` with `--resources` and `--classpath`; the module's Spring Boot tests need Docker for Testcontainers, and are recorded as the tests' result. By hand, `./gradlew :ticketing-service:verifyBoundaries --rerun` with the patch applied reports the route added under its new template with the `!` line and `reads HoldDocument` under it, the old route removed, and `1 problems` in the module's statistics.

The observation specs (`jvmcontract observations --against`, foundations O2), Box Office with this change against Box Office as it is (`lib/tests/observations.rs`, `box_office_examples_compare_as_their_boundary_diffs_say`): `GET /holds/{id}` matches the new `GET /holds/{holdId}` (path variable names aside), and every obligation of the handler is changed. The new spec has a `MissingPathVariableException` with 500 before the handler runs, for every request (from `binding::check`), so its result, exception and status differences begin `the new build answers every request before the handler runs`.

examples.title: HoldExpiredException replaces the ConflictException and no handler maps it: a 500 instead of a 409
examples.summary: The developer gives the expired-hold case of `POST /orders` its own exception, `HoldExpiredException`, carrying the hold id, so that callers and logs can tell it from the other conflicts, and leaves `ApiErrors`, the `@RestControllerAdvice`, as it was. The new class extends `RuntimeException`, not `ConflictException`, so no `@ExceptionHandler` takes it and no `@ResponseStatus` marks it: a client that places an order for an expired hold now gets a 500 from the container's error page instead of the 409 problem detail. The code compiles, the context starts, and the module's unit tests, which call the service and not the route, pass. The boundary contract now lists under each route what it throws and what each exception becomes; the regenerated contract has a `!` line under `POST /orders`: `throws HoldExpiredException: no @ExceptionHandler takes it and it carries no @ResponseStatus, so the response is a 500`.
notes: The first example of the throws lines and the exception outcomes of a boundary contract (`lib/src/failures.rs` for the outcomes, `Graph::throws` in `lib/src/reach.rs` for the exceptions). The exceptions come from the same call graph as the reach lines: a `throw` of a `new`, of a typed local, of what a method returned or a cast produced, the supplier of an `Optional.orElseThrow` (the lambda's return type, or `NoSuchElementException` with no supplier), and Spring's `Assert` (`IllegalStateException` for `state`, `IllegalArgumentException` for the rest). A `catch` on the path that never rethrows its variable swallows what it catches (`HoldService.hold` turns `HoldPolicy`'s `IllegalArgumentException` into `InvalidRequestException` this way); one that does rethrow it, like the retry loop in `Transactions.run` or a `finally`, passes everything through; one that wraps throws the wrapper. An `@Async` callee of another class throws on its own thread. The compiler's own guards, the `MatchException` of an exhaustive switch over a sealed type and an `assert`, are left out.

What each exception becomes follows Spring's resolution order: an `@ExceptionHandler` in the controller (or a superclass of it) first, then the `@ControllerAdvice` beans in `@Order` (ties by class name), each matched by its `basePackages`, `assignableTypes` and `annotations` when it names any, the closest type up the exception's superclass chain winning within one bean; then a `@ResponseStatus` on the exception's class or a superclass; then the status a `ResponseStatusException` was built with, when it is an `HttpStatus` constant. A handler's status is its `@ResponseStatus`, else the first `HttpStatus` constant its body loads (`ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, ...)`), else the literal it passes to `ResponseEntity.status`, else the handler is named without a status. Two `@ExceptionHandler` methods for one type in one advice are a `!` line: Spring refuses the ambiguity when it builds the advice's resolver at startup.

Only an exception type of the module's own (or a sibling module's) that nothing maps is a `!` line. A JDK or framework exception that reaches a route is listed as `(500)` without one: `IllegalStateException` from `Transactions.requireActive` or from a concurrent status change in `OrderTransitions`, `IllegalArgumentException` from `HoldPolicy.totalCents`, are guards, and a 500 is what a guard that fired should be. The regenerated Box Office contracts list these under the routes of the ticketing service (the hold route throws five kinds), with no `!` line: every application exception of the three modules has its handler. What the lines do not see: an exception a framework or driver call throws (`DataAccessException`, `OptimisticLockingFailureException`, a Kafka timeout), a `throws` clause, an exception built in a way the walk cannot type, a handler status computed at run time, and a `ControllerAdvice` ordered by `Ordered` or `@Priority` rather than `@Order`. A `@KafkaListener` or `@Scheduled` method gets its `throws` line without outcomes: the container's error handler (retries, a dead-letter topic, a log line) decides, and that configuration is not read.

The runner compiles the module with Gradle, reads the runtime class path through the build's `printRuntimeClasspath` task, and runs `jvmcontract update` then `verify` with `--resources` and `--classpath`; the module's Spring Boot tests need Docker for Testcontainers, and are recorded as the tests' result. By hand, `./gradlew :ticketing-service:verifyBoundaries --rerun` with the patch applied reports the `POST /orders` route changed, its throws line now ending in `HoldExpiredException (500)` with the `!` line under it, and `1 problems` in the module's statistics.

The observation specs (`jvmcontract observations --against`, foundations O2), Box Office with this change against Box Office as it is (`lib/tests/observations.rs`, `box_office_examples_compare_as_their_boundary_diffs_say`): `POST /orders`: its status is changed. The old build answers 409 for an exception it throws (`ConflictException`, by `ApiErrors.conflict`), and no exception of the new build is answered 409; `HoldExpiredException` is a new outcome with 500 (nothing maps it). The route's normal return builds a `ResponseEntity` whose status is unknown, which is no longer read as hiding the mapping that is gone. In this route the expired hold was the only `ConflictException`, so the 409 is gone entirely.

examples.title: A Retry-After rewritten around two unchanged refill helpers, proved equal in a second
examples.summary: The wait a refused request is told to make is rewritten from `credited + period - now` to `period - (now - credited)`, around the two refill helpers it calls and leaves alone. Each helper holds a 64-bit division, and relating two copies of each across the versions is more than the solver settles in a minute. The proof takes the unchanged helpers as one function in both versions, never sees their arithmetic, and is done in a second.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: equivalent on every input (⚠ stale)
notes: On the machine the examples are measured on (JBMC 6.11.0, CaDiCaL), the proof with the helpers shared took 1.3 s over all 2^320 inputs. With `--no-shared-callees`, the search over inputs in [0:20] passed in a second and the search over [-100000:100000] had not finished after 60 s: two 64-bit divisions and two remainders, one of each per version, compared across the versions.

The helpers are shared because both versions call them, their bytecode is identical in both (constant pool references resolved, so a renumbered pool does not count), and they are pure functions of primitives. A helper that reads a field, takes an array, or calls into the JDK beyond its arithmetic is proved as written, as before.

The stub throws what the helper can throw, here `ArithmeticException` from the division, chosen arbitrarily per new arguments: a version that catches it where the other does not is still found to differ (the library's tests cover that case).

A counterexample found on the stub is replayed through the real bytecode first. One that does not reproduce means the rewrite depends on the helpers' arithmetic; the tool says so in a `note:` line and proves the method again with the helpers as written, which for a 64-bit division may still be the time-out this example avoids.

Since this example was written, the tool's own checker (`--engine native`, examples 124 and 125) proves the change with the helpers as written, in 1.1 s over three paths and three solver calls (0.3 s since the checker leaves a division to the solver under cheap facts and builds its circuit only where a model got it wrong: here never, `0 of 1 divisions and 0 of 0 multiplications built in full` in its log): in it both versions' calls of a helper on the same arguments are the same gates, by the hashing that makes one circuit of one function of the same bits, so the solver never compares two division circuits, which is what the shared-callee stubs achieve for JBMC. That is the library's run of this shape (`--engine native --no-shared-callees`), not the pipeline's; examples 132 and 133 are regression proofs of the refill helper itself by the checker.

Gap scan (step 1a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, 5 November 2026, JDK 25.0.4.1, from the bytecode, nothing proved): the tool's own checker meets no gap in the 3 methods the proof reaches in either version, so strict mode does not move this verdict. The recorded proof is JBMC's, which strict mode of the tool's own checker does not change. JBMC's own approximations are step 4c's.

Unmerged throughout, it found the same witness in 2364 paths with 8907 calls in 1.0 s; merged from the start, in 260 paths with 342 calls in 4.6 s, since each branch of a merged path is a question over every path merged into it and a violation is found only after every path that could reach the join has been merged, where a search going deep first can hit it early. That is why the checker merges only once a search has grown past a few hundred paths, where the paths would otherwise multiply (example 142's note).

examples.title: A short-table scan declared as the intended change, whose proof covers no table at the default bound
examples.summary: The interpreter's `lookupswitch` search gains a linear scan for tables of at most eight pairs, and the regression proof is asked to show the bisection unchanged on the rest: `--unchanged-unless 'matches.length <= 8'`. The default bound on array parameters is eight, so every table in the domain is among the intended inputs, the harness returns before calling either version, and the proof covers no input. The verdict is verified, vacuously, and the tool says so on a line of its own, found by running the statement with the calls replaced by the assertion's failure.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified, vacuously: no input in the domain reaches the calls
notes: The vacuity check is the tool's, whichever engine proved the statement: the probe is run by the tool's own checker over the statement's own domain, and the line appears under a JBMC proof as it does here. It is run only when the harness skips inputs before the calls, that is with `--unchanged-unless`, a record parameter or receiver whose constructor may reject an input, or `--before-arguments` that may throw; a harness that calls the versions on every input has nothing to probe. A `prove` with `--assume` is probed the same way. The probe took 0.0 s here, one path and no solver call, since `matches.length <= 8` is a constant under the bound. Here `python3 examples/tools/build.py` compares the expected verdict with the vacuity too: an example that is verified vacuously must say so in `expected.vacuous`, as the TLC examples of [tag tla-coverage](../README.md#tag-tla-coverage) do.

Why the bound defeats the scope: the scope is over the symbolic array's length, and the domain of a regression proof over arrays is every length up to `--max-array-length`, eight by default, the same number as the scan limit. The proof line prints both, `where !(matches.length <= 8)` and `matches: int[] of length ≤ 8`, and a reader who holds them side by side sees the proof is empty; the tool now holds them side by side for the reader. A scope over the elements can be emptied the same way, by a quantifier that no array up to the bound satisfies, and a scope over scalars by an expression that is a tautology, `skewSeconds >= 0 || skewSeconds < 0`, which is what the check first caught, on example 125's method.

The scan is correct, and the proof that shows it is the one with the sortedness scope, `--unchanged-unless '!(\forall int i; 0 <= i && i < matches.length - 1; matches[i] < matches[i + 1])'`: at bound eight the tool's own checker proves the new `find` equal to the old on every strictly sorted table of up to eight pairs and every key in 1.1 s, 88 paths, 660 solver calls, 46 MB, where the scan runs for every table and the bisection in the previous version; at bound twelve in 3.1 s, 180 paths, 67 MB. Without a scope the checker finds `find(matches=[20, 16], key=16)` in 0.08 s, -1 before (the bisection tests `matches[0] = 20 > 16` and moves `high` below the start) and 1 after (the scan reaches the second pair): on an unsorted table the two searches differ, as example 141 found for the half-open rewrite, and the scope states what every `lookupswitch` table satisfies.

The change is the shape of the JDK's own `DualPivotQuicksort`, which sorts small arrays by insertion sort below a constant threshold, and of many searches that scan short tables rather than bisect them: it is a performance change meant to preserve behaviour, and `behaviourChangeIntended` is false. Declaring the short tables as intended inputs is the mistake this example is about: it is the natural declaration for a reviewer who wants the bisection checked and takes the scan on trust, and it leaves the proof nothing when the bound is the threshold. The domain line of every proof names the bound for this reason.

examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: equivalent on every input outside the declared change

examples.title: A contract that says Random.nextInt never throws is refuted on the JVM before the proof relies on it
examples.summary: Crosscut's retry filter gains full jitter: a wait drawn by `Random.nextInt` below a ceiling the base doubled by a shift kept short of the sign bit with `Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros`. The tool's own checker implements none of the three JDK calls, so under `--gaps advised` the agent driving it writes a contract for each. Its contract for `nextInt` says the call returns a value in [0, bound) and nothing else, which is true wherever this kernel calls it. The tool tests every contract on a real JVM before it relies on one: the JDK's `nextInt` throws `IllegalArgumentException` at `bound=0`, the contract is refused with the JVM's counterexamples, its gap stays open, and the proof stops there, with the other two contracts accepted.
notes: The proof reaches three calls the tool's own checker does not implement, each a gap with an id that names the JDK it is about: `jdk-static-method:java.lang.Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros(I)I@jdk-25.0.4.1`, `jdk-constructor:java.util.Random.<init>(J)V@jdk-25.0.4.1` and `jdk-primitive-method:java.util.Random.nextInt(I)I@jdk-25.0.4.1`. Under `--gaps strict` or `assume` the run would end with no verdict: the two methods return a value the proof reads, which has no assume form. Under `--gaps advised` with no contracts the tool stops before solving with the three gaps, what a contract for each must state, and a template, which is where an agent starts (step 3a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`).

The contracts in `gaps.contracts` were written by an agent, the session that made this example (Claude Opus 5.5), from the template and the JDK's documentation of each call, and are marked so in their `written-by:` lines. Nothing in the library or the runner calls a model: the agent is whoever drives the tool, and the file is committed like any other.

The JVM test is the one that refutes it. The proof against the JDK's bytecode applies only to a static JDK method of primitive parameters, so it covers `numberOfLeadingZeros` and not the two `Random` calls, whose receiver's state it cannot see; those are tested and, at best, `tested`. The test calls `nextInt` on `new java.util.Random()`, the receiver its class's constructor of no arguments builds, since the JDK's `nextInt` throws on its argument alone.

Each of the 84 refuting inputs is a bound of zero or below; the advice keeps the first, `bound=0`, and four more as examples (`-1`, `-2`, `-2147483648`, `-2147483647`). The other 82 inputs return a value in [0, bound), as the contract says.

A contract the JVM refutes is refused even where it would give the right verdict, as here, because the tool cannot know where else it will be applied: example 148's proof, on the corrected contract, is the one that is about this kernel.
