examples.title: A retry throttle rewritten with min and max proved equal on every throttle its constructor makes
examples.summary: Crosscut's retry throttle (gRPC's retry throttling: a failure takes a token, a success gives back the token ratio, retries only while more than half the tokens are left) is a mutable object every call on a channel shares. `recorded` is rewritten in the form gRPC's Java client uses, one clamp with `Math.max` and `Math.min` and the threshold doubled instead of halved. The regression proof takes the throttle as an object made by its constructor from symbolic limits, compares the result and the throttle's fields as both versions leave them, and proves them equal on every input, the claim saying that its throttles are the ones the constructor makes: full ones.
notes: The domain is objects made by their constructor (decision 2 of llm-dlc/loops/foundations.md): `Throttle(ThrottleLimits)` starts full, `maxTokens * 1000` thousandths, so the proof is over one outcome on a full throttle, for every limit the record accepts (1 to 1000 tokens, a ratio of 1 to 1000000 thousandths). A throttle drained by earlier failures is a state no constructor makes; the claim covers none, and its headline and domain say so instead of 'every input'. 152 is the rewrite that differs only there, and is verified by the same proof for the same reason.

Observed: the boolean result, the exception, the throttle's fields as the call leaves them, and the identity relations among the throttle, its limits and the result (`stated.observations.objects` lists `throttle: limits.maxTokens, limits.tokenRatioMilli, milliTokens`). The `ThrottleLimits` record is a value, compared by its components only.

`Math.max` and `Math.min` are taken by the tool's own checker as the JDK computes them, so the proof needs no contract and no JBMC; JBMC cannot take an object input at all (`approach.engine`: native).
Pairs with 151 (the same kernel's `reconfigured`, its alias turned into a copy, refuted) and 152 (this rewrite without the floor at zero, outside the claim).

examples.title: A throttle kept across a config update turned into a copy loses the failures of the calls in flight
examples.summary: When a channel's service config is updated with the same retry limits, `reconfigured` hands back the channel's throttle itself, so the calls in flight, which hold it, keep counting their failures into the throttle the channel goes on using. The change hands back a copy with the same tokens and the same limits instead: every field agrees when it returns, and a failure recorded afterwards by a call in flight goes into the old object, which nothing reads, so a failing backend gets retries the throttle would have refused. The regression proof observes the identity relations within each version and refutes the change with `result == throttle`, which holds before and not after; the witness is a construction recipe, replayed in the interpreter and run on a JVM.
notes: This is the alias-to-copy defect of llm-dlc/loops/foundations.md: an alias turned into a copy with identical primitive values, which a caller sees only by mutating one. Physical object ids are never compared across versions; the identity relation is compared within each version, and the witness's two replays read alike but for it.

The copy reuses the same `ThrottleLimits` object, so `result.limits == throttle.limits` holds in both versions and is no part of the difference; a copy made with `new ThrottleLimits(...)` would differ there too, but a record of primitive components is a value and is compared by components only.

The witness is run on a JVM after the interpreter's replay (`replayed in the interpreter and run on a JVM (JDK …), where the harness fails on it too`): the harness makes each version's throttle from the same leaves, and reads the classes' package-private fields through opened copies of them, which the JVM run loads first on its class path.
Pairs with 150 (the same kernel's `recorded`, rewritten correctly and proved) and 152 (a rewrite of `recorded` that differs only outside the constructor-made domain).

examples.title: A throttle that drops its floor at zero is proved only on full throttles, where it cannot differ
examples.summary: The same rewrite of `recorded` as 150, but the floor at zero tokens is gone: `Math.min(next, ceiling)` without the `Math.max(0, …)`. A failure on a drained throttle now takes it below zero, and every token below zero is ten more successes (at a ratio of 0.1) before the channel may retry again: after three failures on a two-token throttle it takes 21 successes instead of 11. The regression proof verifies the change, because its throttles are made by their constructor, which makes them full, and one failure never drains a full throttle; the verdict says `on every input of constructor-made objects` and the domain names the constructor, so the result is a claim about full throttles only, not a proof that the rewrite is right.
notes: This is the planted defect 'a bug only in a state outside the constructor-made domain, which must show as outside the claim, not as proved' of llm-dlc/loops/foundations.md. The question it answers: can the way inputs are made hide the bug? It can, and so the result names the domain in its headline (`every input of constructor-made objects`, not `every input`), in its domain line, and in its constructible assumption; a reader who takes the verdict as 'the rewrite is right' has dropped those words.

Shown on a JVM by hand, not by the run: `new Throttle(new ThrottleLimits(2, 100))`, three failures, then successes until `recorded` returns true. The unpatched build leaves 1000, 0, 0 thousandths and allows a retry after 11 successes; the patched one 1000, 0, -1000 and 21.
Pairs with 150 (the same rewrite with the floor, proved by the same proof) and 151 (an alias turned into a copy, refuted by an identity relation).

examples.title: A refill helper rewritten as whole periods, proved once and one function in its caller's proof
examples.summary: Crosscut's `TokenBucket.lastAfter`, the time up to which a refill has credited the bucket, is rewritten from `now - (now - last) % period` to `last + (now - last) / period * period`, the whole periods counted and added back. Its caller, the `Retry-After` of a refused request, is unchanged. Run with the proof cache, the regression proof of the caller first proves the helper's two versions equal on every input, as a check of its own, and stores that proof. It then takes the helper as one function in both versions of the caller, whose statement names the helper's proof by its claim key. Where example 120 shares a helper because its bytecode is identical, this one shares a helper that changed, on the strength of its own proof.
notes: Why the proof can take the helper's new version for both: the helper's own proof is over every input of its parameter types, so every call, in either version and with any arguments, is in its domain, and the two versions have the same outcome there, a result or the same exception. Neither reads or writes state. The previous version with its calls redirected therefore behaves exactly as written, and the caller's proof is exact: a counterexample under the redirection would be a real one, and no refinement is needed. A helper proof over a narrower domain (`--unchanged-unless`, mapped arguments, a relation between results) is never used, since it would need an assertion at each call.

Measured when the example was written, on the development machine: the helper's proof took 0.19 s (2 paths, 2 solver calls), and the caller's with the helper as one function 0.00 s (3 paths, 2 solver calls). Without the cache, the caller's proof runs through both versions of the helper as written and takes 1.2 s (4 solver calls) for the same verdict. A second run with the same cache is an exact hit of the caller's claim, and a second caller of the helper would find the helper's proof in the cache. The recorded run starts from an empty cache, so its proof line says the helper was proved now.

The helper's proof is a regression proof like any other, and its key is the one a check of `TokenBucket#lastAfter` alone gets: the library's tests check both, and that a caller's key does not depend on when or where the helper's proof was made.

Without `--cache` the tool proves nothing of a changed helper, and runs the caller through both versions of it, which is what every recorded example did before this one. The cache is the proof's only source of helper evidence, and it is local: a directory under the build, filled by this run and never committed.
Example 161 is the sibling with the helper's change wrong: its own proof is refuted, the helper stays as written, and the caller's proof finds the regression.

Gap scan (step 1a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, 7 November 2026, JDK 25.0.5, from the bytecode, nothing proved): the tool's own checker meets no gap in the 3 methods the proof reaches in either version, so strict mode does not move this verdict.

examples.title: A refill helper aligned to the clock's grid, refuted alone, and its caller sends a client back early
examples.summary: Crosscut's `TokenBucket.lastAfter` is rewritten to credit the bucket up to the start of the period the clock reading falls in, `now - now % period`, as the fixed window aligns its start. A bucket's periods are counted from its last refill, not from the clock's zero, so the credited time moves whenever the last refill is off the clock's grid. Run with the proof cache, the proof first checks the helper on its own and refutes it, so the helper stays as written in both versions. The helper's own counterexample lies outside the module's precondition, with the clock reading before the last refill, since the helper's proof covers every input and the shrinker keeps the smallest. examples.title: A quote's amount made a value object, proved at its route and in its kernel with no mapping written

The tool compares the two builds whole: the route `POST /quotes` answers the same total and sends the same event on every request, and the kernel's `total` and `withQuantity` do what they did under a relation between the old and new quotes that it inferred itself; the rewritten helper is proved once and used as one function in `total`'s proof, and a rerun is an exact hit of every proof.
notes: Checked by `jvmcontract compare`, which build.py runs as the B9 check of the shop app (`run_tool_compare`): the unpatched build against the patched one, twice under one fresh proof cache, the verdict read from the rerun and the page's output from the first run. The verdict is the subject's; the page lists every other part the run checked.

The joint example of `llm-dlc/loops/foundations.md`'s Phase 5, made an example: the app's sources are the fixture's `before` build (`lib/tests/fixtures/foundations/`), and the patch turns them into its `after` build. `lib/tests/compare.rs` holds `jvmcontract compare` to the same builds inline; this is the same run by build.py, with the app's tests run too.

Nothing in the run is written by hand. The entry points' external inputs (`cents`, `quantity`) are anchored by their observation specs, so no mapping is involved at the boundary.
